newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian race row MP vows to fight on.
newsitem.headline: Australian race row MP vows to fight on.

text.p: Australian race row politician Pauline Hanson vowed on Tuesday to continue rallying support for her One Nation party, despite violent protests that have left several people injured.

Two protesters were arrested at a rowdy anti-Hanson demonstration in the Australian capital on Tuesday night, a day after another launch meeting for Hanson's One Nation party descended into violence in a country town near Melbourne.
Hanson said that those who attacked her party's meeting in the rural town of Dandenong outside Melbourne on Monday were "political terrorists", and declared she would not back down.

"It is getting worse," Hanson said in a television interview. "All they are, are political terrorists. I never wanted it (the violence), but it makes me more determined, and people around me are more determined, that we have to stop this sort of growing violence that is happening in Australia."
"You must to stand up for your rights."
Asked if she feared someone might be killed at a One Nation rally, Hanson said: "Yes, but are we going to live in fear for the rest of our lives?"

Police said on Tuesday that two people had been arrested after protests against a One Nation launch meeting at Canberra's National Press Club. One of them was accused of assaulting police officers and the other of disturbing the peace.

Up to 2,000 protesters gathered outside the meeting chanting "racist scum" and "racists go home" as just over 100 Hanson supporters arrived for the meeting, which Hanson herself -- a Queensland independent who has attracted a nation-wide following on an anti-immigration platform -- did not attend.

Protesters were kept behind barricades across the street, preventing a repeat of the more serious violence at a One Nation meeting in the Victorian town of Dandenong on Monday. There, several people were injured including a 60-year-old Hanson supporter who was taken to hospital with head injuries.
Up to 1,500 protesters disrupted the Dandenong meeting, which was attended 150 Hanson supporters but not by Hanson.
Police said a small militant group of protesters, some wearing balaclavas, threw potatoes, eggs and urine-filled balloons at Hanson supporters.

But protest organiser Peter Jolly said the protest was peaceful until police and One Nation bodyguards moved into the crowd. "We are not in favour of rioting and bashing. We say it is One Nation which started that last night," Jolly said.
A former Australian deputy prime minister, Jim Cairns, 82, joined in the protests but was thrown out of the meeting after he started distributing anti-Hanson tracts.
Police said they would tighten up security at a country rally to be attended by Hanson next week in Geelong, another Victorian country town.
One Nation, which also campaigns against Aboriginal welfare, has attracted support away from Australia's main political parties to become the country's third political force.

An opinion poll on Tuesday showed six-percent support for the independent politician and her party, which was only officially registered last month. Hanson is the only elected member of her party, which has yet to be tested at an election.
